title: The Shop
strapline: Baskets, bananas and 'that'll be three pounds please' — maths you can put in a bag.
intent: Shopping is the everyday maths children already know from real life: counting things into a basket, handing over coins, hearing 'how much?' and 'have we got enough?'
Stocking and running a shop means sorting and organising — fruit with fruit, tins with tins — and noticing when the shelf is empty.
Environmental print does real work here: shop signs, price labels, open/closed signs, logos children recognise from their own high street.
The counter is a stage for real exchanges — greeting customers, asking for what you want, saying thank you.
Queuing, waiting and taking your turn at the till are fairness in action.
The play connects to children's own community — the shops they visit, the shopkeepers who know them.
implementation: Be a customer with problems to solve: 'I need four apples and I've only got three coins — what shall I do?'
Model shop language until children own it: 'anything else?', 'that'll be two pounds', 'sorry, we've sold out.'
Price things in small honest numbers (1p–5p) so the maths stays within reach — and count coins into hands slowly, one by one.
Involve children in making the print: shop signs, price tickets, open/closed signs, special-offer posters.
Restock together and think aloud about sorting: 'where do the tins live? How many bananas are left?'
Walk to a real local shop with a short list, then watch the detail flood back into the role play.
Stand back at the queue: waiting a turn at the till is a chance to practise fairness, not a problem to manage away.
key_questions: What do you need today? How many shall I put in your bag?
How much does this cost? Have you got enough pennies?
We've sold out of milk — what could we do?
Where should the new stock go so customers can find it?
Who serves you at the shops near your house?

impact.text: Children set up and replay shop scenes — filling baskets, ringing the till, bagging up — holding a real back-and-forth exchange across the counter.
Children count items into baskets and coins into hands one by one, knowing the last number tells them how many.
Children sort the stock — fruit together, tins together — and spot what's the same, what's different and what's missing.
Children compare amounts and prices in play — 'that costs more', 'there's not many left', 'this bag is really full'.
Children notice and use the print around the shop — signs, labels, logos they know from their own high street.
Children write shopping lists, price tickets and signs, and read them back to customers.
Children wait their turn in the queue and at the till — increasingly without an adult holding the line.
Children connect the play to real shopkeepers and the shops on their own street, retelling what happens there.

enhancements: Real (clean, empty) packets and tins from families' kitchens, reflecting everyone's food cupboards.
Real 1p and 2p coins in the till, with small purses and wallets.
A working balance scale for weighing fruit and veg.
Blank price tickets, a clipboard 'stock list' and pens at the counter.
A market-stall day outdoors: crates, a canopy and loud 'fresh strawberries!' calls.
Paper bags and baskets so packing purchases becomes part of the job.
A trip to the greengrocer or corner shop with a real list and real money.

playing_exploring: Children replay an errand they've done a hundred times with a grown-up — now they hold the money and the power.
The till, scales and coins invite hands-on investigation before any storyline starts.
active_learning: Getting served, paying and packing your own bag is a satisfying sequence children see through to the end — then queue up to do again.
creating_thinking: Children solve real shop problems their own way — sold out of milk, a customer with no money, a shelf that won't stay tidy.
